title: Is a Foreign Divorce Valid in Bangladesh? Talaq Registration for NRBs in the UK and USA
metaTitle: Foreign Divorce Valid in Bangladesh? NRB Talaq Guide
metaDescription: Is a UK or US divorce valid in Bangladesh? How talaq notice, registration and foreign decrees work for NRBs, plus dower, custody and bigamy risks.
heroIntro: A UK or US divorce decree, or a talaq pronounced in front of a local imam, does not always end a marriage in the eyes of Bangladeshi law, offices and courts. This pillar guide explains how section 7 of the Muslim Family Laws Ordinance 1961, the Registration Act 1974, the Dissolution of Muslim Marriages Act 1939 and section 13 of the Code of Civil Procedure 1908 fit together for NRBs. It is written by Advocate Md. Shah Alam, Supreme Court of Bangladesh, for Bangladeshis living in the UK, USA, UAE, Canada and elsewhere. For case-specific help call or WhatsApp the chamber on 01712655546.

quickAnswer.heading: Foreign Divorce in Bangladesh
points: A foreign court decree may be recognised in Bangladesh under CPC section 13 and private international law, but it is not automatic and can be challenged.
Under section 7 of the Muslim Family Laws Ordinance 1961, talaq needs written notice to the Chairman and the wife, and takes effect after 90 days unless revoked.
A foreign decree alone does not update the Nikah register, NID or passport records in Bangladesh.
Dower (denmohor), maintenance and child custody claims survive a foreign divorce.
Remarrying without finishing the Bangladeshi steps can expose a person to a bigamy complaint.
Check current attestation, apostille and fee rules with the Bangladesh Mission and the relevant office.

sections.h2: Short Answer: Is a Foreign Divorce Valid in Bangladesh?
sections.content:
Many Bangladeshis in the UK, USA, Canada, Australia and the Gulf assume that once a foreign court has granted a divorce, or a husband has pronounced talaq in front of a local imam, the marriage is over everywhere. In practice the position is more layered. A divorce can be valid in the country where it was granted and still be uncertain, incomplete or unrecorded in Bangladesh.

The honest short answer is this: a foreign decree may be recognised by a Bangladeshi court under the principles of private international law and section 13 of the Code of Civil Procedure 1908, but recognition is not automatic, it can be challenged, and a foreign decree on its own does not change any Bangladeshi record. For Muslim spouses, the safest route is usually to combine the foreign divorce with a talaq notice and registration under Bangladeshi law, so that the marriage is closed on both sides of the world.

This guide is a deeper pillar for NRBs. If you want the general overview first, read our shorter pieces on overseas divorce for NRBs and the divorce procedure for probashi Bangladeshis. For the wider set of services, see the NRB legal help hub.

sections.h2: Which Law Applies to Your Marriage?
sections.content:
Bangladesh has no single uniform divorce law. Family matters are governed by personal law, which depends on the religion of the parties:

  • Muslims: Muslim personal law as modified by the Muslim Family Laws Ordinance 1961, the Muslim Marriages and Divorces (Registration) Act 1974 and its Rules, and the Dissolution of Muslim Marriages Act 1939. Family Courts hear disputes about dissolution, dower, maintenance and custody.
  • Christians: the Divorce Act 1869 and related Christian marriage legislation.
  • Hindus and others: largely governed by religious and customary law, with limited statutory provisions. This is a specialised area and needs individual advice.

Section 1 of the Muslim Family Laws Ordinance 1961 states that it applies to Muslim citizens of Bangladesh. The wording of the original text extends it to citizens wherever they may be. This is one reason Bangladeshi authorities and courts may still expect a Muslim husband who is a Bangladeshi citizen living in London or New York to follow the notice procedure of section 7, even after a foreign court or imam has acted. Whether and how a court applies that to a particular person (for example someone who has given up Bangladeshi citizenship or is domiciled abroad) is a question of fact and law that should be checked with an advocate.

sections.h2: Talaq Under Section 7 of the Muslim Family Laws Ordinance 1961
sections.content:
Section 7 is the heart of talaq law in Bangladesh. In plain terms, as generally understood:

  1. A Muslim man who wants to divorce his wife by talaq must give written notice of the talaq to the Chairman (for a rural area, the Chairman of the Union Parishad; for urban areas, the relevant Mayor or City Corporation / Paurashava authority, as defined in the Ordinance and subsequent local government law).
  2. He must also send a copy of the notice to the wife.
  3. Unless the talaq is revoked, it does not become effective until 90 days after the day on which the notice is delivered to the Chairman. If the wife is pregnant at the end of that period, the rule is that the talaq takes effect only after the pregnancy ends.
  4. Within a set period after receiving the notice, the Chairman is required to form an Arbitration Council to try to bring about reconciliation between the spouses.
  5. A man who pronounces talaq and fails to give the required notice faces a criminal penalty under the Ordinance. Check the current text of the section for the exact penalty.

Two points matter for NRBs. First, a pronouncement of talaq (orally, by text message, by email or in front of a foreign imam) does not by itself satisfy section 7. The notice and the waiting period are the legal mechanism. Second, the 90-day period runs from delivery of the notice to the Chairman, not from the day the husband spoke the words or signed a foreign document.

If you want to see how this process works inside Bangladesh, read our Bengali guides on the talaq notice procedure and the rules for writing a talaqnama.

Registration of divorce is dealt with by the Muslim Marriages and Divorces (Registration) Act 1974 and its Rules, which provide for records kept by licensed Nikah Registrars (Kazis). The practical idea is that the Nikah Registrar of the area where the marriage was registered or where the wife lives should have a record of the talaq. Procedures, forms and fees are set by the current Rules and local offices, so confirm them directly.

sections.h2: How Bangladesh Treats Foreign Court Decrees (CPC Section 13)
sections.content:
When a foreign court (for example an English court or a US state court) grants a divorce, a Bangladeshi court asks whether it should treat that decree as binding. The general framework is found in the principles of private international law and in section 13 of the Code of Civil Procedure 1908.

Section 13 says that a foreign judgment is conclusive on any matter it directly decided between the same parties, except in certain situations. As commonly summarised, a foreign judgment will not be treated as conclusive where it:

  • was not pronounced by a court of competent jurisdiction;
  • was not given on the merits of the case;
  • appears on its face to be founded on an incorrect view of international law, or on a refusal to recognise Bangladeshi law where that law applied;
  • was obtained in proceedings contrary to natural justice (for example the other spouse was never properly notified or had no chance to be heard);
  • was obtained by fraud; or
  • sustains a claim founded on a breach of a law in force in Bangladesh.

Section 14 adds that a court presumes, unless the contrary appears, that a certified copy of a foreign judgment was pronounced by a court of competent jurisdiction. This is why a properly certified copy of the decree matters.

For a Muslim couple who are Bangladeshi by origin, the hard questions are usually about jurisdiction and natural justice: Was the foreign court a proper forum for these spouses? Was the spouse in Bangladesh served properly and given a real chance to respond? Did the court apply a law that Bangladeshi law would regard as acceptable for the marriage? Because the answer depends on the facts, treat any statement that a foreign decree is "always valid" or "never valid" in Bangladesh with caution. Recognition is normally decided by a Bangladeshi court if the point is contested, for example in a dower suit, a maintenance claim, an inheritance dispute or a criminal complaint of bigamy.

sections.h2: Recognition Table: UK Decree, US Decree, Talaq Abroad and Khula
sections.content:
The table below is a practical summary of how the main routes are usually viewed. It is a general guide only. Each case depends on its facts, and a Bangladeshi court always has the final word if the matter is contested.

RouteValid where granted?Position in BangladeshRecommended extra step for Muslim spouses
UK court divorce (final order / decree absolute)Yes, once the final order is made.May be recognised under CPC section 13 and private international law, but it is open to challenge on jurisdiction, notice or fraud. It does not update Bangladeshi records by itself.Send a section 7 talaq notice (if the husband is the divorcing party) and register the divorce with the Nikah Registrar, or obtain legal advice on a declaration.
US court divorce (final judgment of dissolution)Yes, under the law of the relevant US state once final.Same analysis as above. A certified copy of the final judgment is the key document.Same as above. Keep proof that the other spouse was properly served.
Talaq pronounced abroad (orally, by message, or before a mosque or imam, with no court)Often not a recognised legal divorce in the UK or in most US states unless a court process follows. Check local law.Not effective under section 7 unless notice is given to the Chairman and 90 days pass (without revocation). The husband risks penalty for not giving notice.Give the section 7 notice properly, send a copy to the wife, and register with the Nikah Registrar.
Khula (wife seeks release, by agreement or by court)Depends on how it was obtained. A court process abroad is generally treated as a court divorce. A purely religious khula may have no legal effect abroad.Judicial dissolution in Bangladesh is under the Dissolution of Muslim Marriages Act 1939 read with Family Court procedure. A khula by agreement should be documented, and the dower position stated clearly.Put the agreement in writing, note what happens to dower and maintenance, and consider a Family Court decree or registration.

The consistent message is that a foreign route and a Bangladeshi route are not alternatives to each other if you want certainty. They work best together.

sections.h2: Why a UK or US Decree Alone May Not Update Bangladeshi Records
sections.content:
A foreign divorce decree is a document of a foreign court. Bangladeshi government offices do not automatically receive it, and no international system sends it to Dhaka. This is the main reason spouses discover years later that they are still shown as married in Bangladeshi records.

  • Nikah register: The marriage entry kept by the Nikah Registrar and the local registers remain unchanged unless a divorce is recorded there. A later buyer, bank, embassy or court that checks the register may still find a subsisting marriage.
  • NID: The National Identity Card database records marital status in some cases. A change usually needs a formal correction application with supporting documents, not just a foreign decree.
  • Passport: A Bangladeshi passport may carry a spouse name. Updating or reissuing requires the passport office's own documentary requirements, which can change.
  • Court record: If the spouse in Bangladesh later files a case for dower, maintenance, restitution of conjugal rights or inheritance, the court will examine whether the foreign decree should be treated as binding.
  • Immigration and sponsorship: A foreign immigration authority may accept a local decree, but a Bangladeshi visa, marriage registration or sponsorship may be affected by a mismatch between records.

None of this means your foreign divorce is worthless. It means that for Bangladesh you usually need an additional step, either a talaq notice with registration or a court declaration, so that the paper trail matches the foreign decree.

sections.h2: How to Send a Talaq Notice or Register a Foreign Divorce from Abroad
sections.content:
If you are the Muslim husband and you are abroad, the safest way to protect yourself is usually to follow the Bangladeshi procedure in addition to any foreign process.

  1. Prepare a written notice of talaq. It should name both spouses, give the date and place of the marriage, and be signed by the husband. Many people have it notarised, or attested at the Bangladesh Mission, so that the signature is easy to prove.
  2. Address the notice to the correct Chairman. This is generally the authority for the area where the wife resides (or, in some cases, where the marriage was registered). Confirm the right office with an advocate or by contacting the Union Parishad or City Corporation, because areas and office names have changed over time.
  3. Send a copy to the wife. Use a method that gives proof of delivery, such as registered post or courier with a receipt.
  4. Keep proof of delivery to the Chairman and to the wife. The 90-day period is counted from delivery to the Chairman, so the delivery date matters.
  5. Respond to the Arbitration Council. If the Chairman constitutes a council and calls the parties, take part through a representative or in writing. Ignoring the council can create problems later.
  6. After the waiting period, ask for a certificate or record that the talaq has taken effect and have it entered with the Nikah Registrar, following the Registration Act 1974 and its Rules.
  7. Update records (NID, passport and any property or visa records) using the registered divorce document.

Whether a husband can send the notice through an attorney or advocate, and exactly how a Chairman will treat a notice posted from overseas, depends on the individual office and current practice. Ask for the office's requirements in writing and do not rely on hearsay. If the divorce was initiated by the wife (for example through a delegated right of talaq recorded in the marriage contract, or through khula or judicial dissolution), the steps differ and legal advice is important.

Use this checklist as a working plan. Tick each item before you consider the divorce complete for Bangladeshi purposes.

  1. Identify your personal law. Muslim, Christian, Hindu or other. Note your citizenship and where you are domiciled.
  2. Collect the marriage documents. Kabinnama (marriage contract), Nikah registration record, any marriage certificate from abroad and passport copies of both spouses.
  3. Obtain the foreign divorce papers. Certified copy of the final order or judgment, with proof of service on the other spouse and the full court file if available.
  4. Decide who is divorcing whom. Talaq by husband, khula or judicial divorce initiated by wife, or mutual consent. The Bangladeshi route depends on this.
  5. Serve the section 7 talaq notice (for Muslim husbands) on the Chairman and the wife, and keep proof.
  6. Wait out the statutory period and engage with any Arbitration Council notice.
  7. Register the divorce with the Nikah Registrar and obtain a copy of the entry.
  8. Check attestation requirements. Confirm current apostille or legalisation rules for your foreign documents with the Ministry of Foreign Affairs and the Bangladesh Mission.
  9. Settle dower and maintenance. Pay or document the unpaid dower, iddat maintenance and any child maintenance, and keep receipts.
  10. Record child arrangements. Custody, residence and travel consent, ideally in a court order or a written agreement.
  11. Update your records. NID, passport, bank and property documents, and tell the foreign immigration authority where relevant.
  12. Do not remarry in Bangladesh or abroad until you have confirmed that both the foreign and Bangladeshi steps are complete.

Foreign documents used in Bangladesh usually need to be shown to be genuine. This may involve notarisation, authentication by the foreign ministry of the country that issued the document, and then attestation by a Bangladesh Mission, or an apostille where a country and the destination are both parties to the relevant convention. Rules on apostille and legalisation for documents going into Bangladesh have been changing. Check the current apostille and legalisation requirements with the Ministry of Foreign Affairs of Bangladesh and the Bangladesh Mission in your country before you start, and ask for the requirement in writing.

Typical documents that may need attestation include:

  • Certified copy of the final decree or judgment of divorce;
  • Proof that the other spouse was served or took part;
  • Any marriage certificate issued abroad;
  • Powers of attorney authorising someone in Bangladesh to act for you (see our guide on the power of attorney procedure, in Bengali);
  • Identity and passport pages, translated into Bengali or English where required.

Keep both the originals and several certified copies. Courts and offices in Bangladesh may ask for translation, and an incomplete chain of attestation is one of the commonest reasons a foreign document is refused.

sections.h2: Dower, Maintenance and Child Custody After a Foreign Divorce
sections.content:
A foreign divorce does not erase the financial and parental duties that arise from a Bangladeshi Muslim marriage. These survive and can be claimed separately.

  • Dower (denmohor): Unpaid prompt or deferred dower remains a debt owed by the husband. A wife can claim it in a Family Court in Bangladesh even if a foreign decree has ended the marriage. See our guide on claiming dower and maintenance from abroad.
  • Maintenance: Maintenance during the marriage, maintenance for the iddat (waiting) period, and maintenance for the children continue to be enforceable according to law. The amounts are for the court to decide on the facts.
  • Child custody and guardianship: Disputes are decided by the Family Court with the welfare of the child as the main test, using the Guardians and Wards Act 1890 and Muslim personal law. A foreign custody order may be considered, but it does not bind a Bangladeshi court automatically. Read child custody when a parent lives abroad and, in Bengali, the custody and guardianship guide.
  • Taking a child abroad: Removing a child from Bangladesh or from the other parent without agreement or a court order can lead to serious legal consequences. Always get consent or an order first.

If you or your spouse have a foreign spouse or children with foreign citizenship, see also marriage registration for NRBs with a foreign spouse.

sections.h2: Remarriage Risk: Bigamy Exposure if the Divorce Is Not Registered
sections.content:
The most serious practical risk of an unregistered divorce is remarriage. If Bangladeshi law treats the first marriage as still subsisting, a second marriage can expose a person to criminal and civil consequences:

  • Penal Code section 494 deals with marrying again during the lifetime of a husband or wife. A first spouse in Bangladesh may file a complaint, and the question whether the first marriage had ended can become the central issue in the case.
  • Muslim Family Laws Ordinance 1961, section 6 restricts a second marriage during the subsistence of the first without written permission from the Arbitration Council, and provides for consequences if the rule is ignored.
  • Civil effects: inheritance, property and legitimacy disputes, and difficulty registering the second marriage or sponsoring a new spouse.

A foreign decree may be a strong defence in such a case, but a defendant should not have to rely on arguing recognition only after being arrested or sued. Completing the Bangladeshi steps before remarriage greatly reduces this risk. For the criminal angle, see our Bengali guides on second marriage without talaq and section 494.

sections.h2: Christian, Hindu and Other Parties: A High-Level Note
sections.content:
Everything above about section 7 talaq and Nikah Registrar entries applies to Muslim marriages. If you are not Muslim:

  • Christians: Divorce is governed by the Divorce Act 1869, which sets out grounds and the court process. A foreign decree may be considered under CPC section 13 in the same way, and records kept by the relevant church or registrar may also need updating.
  • Hindus: The position is mainly governed by religious and customary law, and statutory provisions on divorce are limited. Recognition of a foreign divorce between Bangladeshi Hindus can be complicated and should be checked with a qualified advocate.
  • Mixed-religion or foreign-spouse marriages: The law that applies to the marriage and to its end depends on where and how it was celebrated. Professional advice is strongly recommended.

In all cases the same practical rule applies: obtain a certified copy of the foreign decree, check what Bangladeshi record needs updating, and do not assume that the foreign decree alone is enough.

• Treating a verbal talaq or WhatsApp message as a complete divorce. Section 7 requires written notice to the Chairman and a waiting period.
  • Counting 90 days from the date of the foreign decree, instead of from delivery of notice to the Chairman.
  • Not sending a copy to the wife. A notice that never reached her is easy to attack later.
  • Assuming a UK or US decree is automatically recorded in Bangladesh. It is not. Records must be updated by application.
  • Remarrying before the Bangladeshi steps are finished, and then facing a bigamy complaint.
  • Ignoring the Arbitration Council notice, which can lead to adverse findings or delay.
  • Forgetting dower and maintenance. A divorce does not wipe out unpaid denmohor.
  • Using poor translations or unattested documents, which offices and courts may reject.
  • Not keeping proof of delivery of the notice or the foreign service papers.
  • Paying an unlicensed agent who promises a quick registration without a real record. Always verify the entry in the actual Nikah register.

This article is general legal information, not legal advice. Laws, forms, fees and office practice change, and the outcome of any divorce question depends on your religion, citizenship, domicile, the court that granted the decree and the documents you hold. Confirm the current rules with the relevant office or a qualified advocate before acting.

This is a general guide for Bangladeshis abroad and not a substitute for advice on your own documents. If a case is pending in a foreign or Bangladeshi court, or a criminal complaint has been filed, get individual legal advice promptly. For related help, see the NRB legal help hub.

faqs.question: Is a UK or US court divorce valid in Bangladesh?
faqs.answer: It may be recognised by a Bangladeshi court under private international law and section 13 of the Code of Civil Procedure 1908, but it is not automatic. It can be challenged on grounds such as jurisdiction, lack of proper notice or fraud, and it does not update Bangladeshi records by itself.

faqs.question: Is talaq pronounced in the UK or USA valid in Bangladesh?
faqs.answer: Under section 7 of the Muslim Family Laws Ordinance 1961, a talaq becomes effective only after written notice is given to the Chairman and the wife and the 90-day period passes without revocation. A spoken or messaged talaq alone does not satisfy that. Its legal status in the UK or US also depends on local law, so check both.

faqs.question: How long does talaq take to become effective?
faqs.answer: Under section 7, generally 90 days from the day the notice reaches the Chairman, and if the wife is pregnant, after the pregnancy ends if that is later. The 90 days do not run from the date of a foreign decree.

faqs.question: Can I send the talaq notice from abroad?
faqs.answer: Yes, the notice can generally be prepared and sent from abroad in writing, with proof of delivery to the Chairman and the wife. The exact way a local office treats an overseas notice varies, so confirm the requirements and consider using an advocate.

faqs.question: Do I need an apostille or attestation for my divorce papers?
faqs.answer: Foreign documents often need notarisation, authentication and attestation, or an apostille where applicable. Rules have been changing, so check the current apostille and legalisation requirements with the Ministry of Foreign Affairs and the Bangladesh Mission.

faqs.question: Does my wife still get dower and maintenance after a foreign divorce?
faqs.answer: Yes. Unpaid dower (denmohor) remains a debt, and maintenance rights, including iddat and child maintenance, are not erased by a foreign decree. A wife can claim in a Bangladeshi Family Court.

faqs.question: Can I remarry if I only have a foreign divorce decree?
faqs.answer: It is risky. If Bangladeshi law or the other spouse treats the first marriage as continuing, a second marriage can lead to a bigamy complaint under Penal Code section 494 and issues under section 6 of the Muslim Family Laws Ordinance. Complete the Bangladeshi steps first.

faqs.question: Will a foreign custody order be enforced in Bangladesh?
faqs.answer: A Bangladeshi Family Court decides custody on the welfare of the child. It may consider a foreign order, but is not bound by it automatically.

faqs.question: What if my wife started the divorce?
faqs.answer: A wife may end the marriage through a delegated right of talaq recorded in the marriage contract, through khula, or through judicial dissolution under the Dissolution of Muslim Marriages Act 1939. The steps and records differ, so take legal advice.
